title: Het Winkeltje: an abandoned shop in Belgium
paragraphs: Het Winkeltje is an abandoned Belgian shop with a house above it and remnants of stock still inside. Those everyday objects make it a compelling subject for urbex photography: a glimpse of a business that once served its neighbourhood.

By my visit in May 2021, the building had already suffered considerable damage. Even so, the shop’s original purpose was still visible. Choosing the right angles helped me bring the surviving details into focus.
The rooms upstairs were in an even more damaged state. These photographs record what remained at the time, before more of the building’s character could disappear.

title: Ferme aux Drapeaux: photographing an abandoned Belgian farm
paragraphs: Ferme aux Drapeaux was the second stop on my urbex photography trip to Belgium, after Maison Milka. Its large farmhouse and courtyard offered original doors, weathered interiors and plenty of details to photograph.

Flags hanging in the living room explain the name, which translates as “Flag Farm”. In a shed, we nearly overlooked an unexpected subject: a blue Barkas B1000 camper van, built in East Germany. I wondered how it had ended up here.

We met another pair of photographers exploring the building. Between the farmhouse interiors, the vehicle and the remains of life in the stables, this was one of the most memorable locations of the trip.

title: Maison Milka: an urbex photo essay in Belgium
paragraphs: After more than a year of limited photography during the pandemic, I travelled to Belgium to explore abandoned places. Urbex photography had been on my list for some time. Maison Milka was the first stop.

From the street, the house looked ordinary, with little to suggest the condition of its interior. The rooms had already suffered damage, but furniture and objects left behind still offered interesting subjects.
The attic was particularly atmospheric. The photographs focus on those remaining details: an old bed, shoes, a coat and other traces of the life the house once contained.

title: Tel Aviv and Jerusalem: coastal light and old city streets
paragraphs: A business trip to Israel gave me the opportunity to photograph two very different cities: Tel Aviv on the Mediterranean coast and Jerusalem, with its historic streets and religious landmarks.
In Tel Aviv, I reached the beach in time for a colourful sunset. The open coastline offered a change of pace from the streets and buildings of the city.

In Jerusalem, our walk took us from the Mount of Olives into the old city and along the Via Dolorosa. This small collection brings together the coastal evening light and the textures of Jerusalem’s streets.

title: The Julian Alps: lakes and landscapes of Slovenia
paragraphs: Slovenia’s Julian Alps offered far more than the churches, waterfalls and gorges we had planned to photograph. Around Triglav National Park, we repeatedly stopped for mountain views, clear water and quiet countryside.

One memorable stop was the spring feeding the Sava river, where remarkably clear water revealed movement beneath the surface. Lake Bohinj offered another mountain setting, very different from nearby Lake Bled.

Forests and carefully kept meadows connected these larger landmarks. We also hoped to see brown bears during the trip, but none appeared. Even without them, there was no shortage of landscapes worth bringing home.

title: Vintgar and Tolmin: photographing Slovenia’s gorges
paragraphs: Vintgar Gorge and Tolmin Gorge were two highlights of our journey through Slovenia’s Julian Alps. Both offered clear water, dramatic rock walls and very different experiences behind the camera.
We arrived at Vintgar as it opened. For roughly half an hour, the walkway was quiet enough to photograph with few people in the frame. Later, the growing crowds made that much harder.

Tolmin felt more varied, with different corners to explore rather than one main route. That spread visitors out and gave us more breathing room. I enjoyed both, although Vintgar’s scenery made the stronger impression on me.

title: Waterfalls of Slovenia: six stops in the Julian Alps
paragraphs: Our trip through the Julian Alps took us to six Slovenian waterfalls: Peričnik, Savica, Peračica, Boka, Kozjak and Grmečica. Each had a different setting and its own photographic character.
We visited during hot weather, when the flow was lower than we had hoped. That changed the scale of some falls, but also made it interesting to look for smaller details and quieter compositions.
For a return trip, I would like to see the region in spring, when melting mountain snow may bring more water. This collection records the waterfalls as we found them during our summer visit.

title: Hilltop churches in the Slovenian landscape
paragraphs: Small white churches punctuate Slovenia’s countryside. Often standing on hilltops, they give the surrounding fields, forests and mountains a clear focal point.

We photographed Sveti Tomaž, Sveti Jakob, St Peter above Begunje, St Primož and the church on Lake Bled’s island. We also stopped at less familiar churches beside the road, sometimes without knowing their names.

I enjoyed the relationship between the buildings and the landscape as much as the architecture itself. This series follows those encounters, from well-known viewpoints to unplanned roadside discoveries.

title: Lake Bled photography: island views and sunset light
paragraphs: Lake Bled combines clear water, a mountain backdrop and a small island with a distinctive church. It was one of the places I most wanted to photograph during our trip to Slovenia.

We visited in summer, when the lakeside was busy. Climbing to the Ojstrica and Mala Osojnica viewpoints changed the perspective completely: from above, the island and surrounding landscape took centre stage.

Later, we returned to the water for sunset. The different viewpoints and changing light made it possible to photograph the same lake in several ways, from wide mountain scenes to quieter evening reflections.

title: Lohagad Fort near Pune: a mountain photography trek
paragraphs: While staying in Pune for work, I made an early-morning trip to Lohagad Fort. Leaving at 5 am helped us avoid some city traffic and begin the climb before the day became too hot.
The journey was eventful: our car nearly broke down on the way, and monkeys greeted us near the village and along the route. We kept our belongings close while climbing the old, slippery steps.

From the fort, the views revealed how the walls stretch across the mountain. The monsoon was only beginning, so much of the landscape was still brown and grey rather than green. Even so, the scale of the setting made the trek worthwhile.

title: De Terp in Leidschenveen: a white landmark on a green hill
paragraphs: De Terp in Leidschenveen looks like a small chapel on a grassy hill. In fact, it is an artwork designed by Laurens Kolks and erected in 2009, close to my home in Zoetermeer.

The white building and green slope create a surprisingly remote-looking scene. From a distance, I could almost imagine it in Scandinavia or in a film landscape. Up close, the structure is smaller than it first appears and has no religious symbols.
Ordinary streets and dog walkers surround the site. Finding a composition that emphasised the hill and building was a reminder that distinctive photographs do not always require a long journey.

title: Dubai from The Palm: Atlantis and the Jumeirah skyline
paragraphs: During our 2019 stay on Palm Jumeirah, I photographed two very different waterfront views: the Jumeirah coastline and the distinctive Atlantis hotel.

The private beach at Fairmont The Palm provided the first viewpoint, looking back towards the city. For Atlantis, I photographed from The Pointe, which offered an open view across the water during our visit.
The two settings brought together the scale of Dubai’s skyline and the character of one of its most recognisable hotels. These photographs record the waterfront as it looked on that trip.

title: Meijendel Beach: a winter walk at sunset
paragraphs: Meijendel is a nature reserve I return to for its combination of woodland, dunes and beach. On this February visit, I explored the area with my five-year-old son, who followed me through the rough terrain without complaint.

We reached the beach around sunset, just in time to photograph the changing coastal light. There was an unexpected detail on the sand: hundreds of stranded starfish. We walked carefully to avoid them.
The quieter winter atmosphere gave the beach a different character from my earlier visits to the woodland and dunes. Together, those outings show how much variety this stretch of coast offers.

title: Budapest Parliament at night: golden reflections on the Danube
paragraphs: The illuminated Hungarian Parliament Building was an essential stop on my Budapest photography trip. From the opposite bank of the Danube, its lights cast a striking golden reflection across the river.

Getting a clear view took patience. A moored boat blocked the composition we wanted, and other vessels regularly passed through the frame. Just before leaving, we returned to find a short opening. A few minutes later, the boat was back.

Above the building, tiny lights looked almost like falling stars. They turned out to be birds catching the floodlights. Although they do not show in this photograph, they added another memorable detail to the evening.

title: Mastbos in autumn: mushrooms and Bouvigne Castle
paragraphs: An autumn walk through the Mastbos near Breda became a study of mushrooms rather than the wider forest. The seasonal colours had not quite peaked, and forestry work made some woodland compositions difficult.
The smaller subjects more than made up for it. We found beautifully formed fly agarics, whose colours and shapes stood out against the forest floor.

Nearby Bouvigne Castle offered a different subject at the end of the outing. Its setting worked particularly well during blue hour, adding an architectural contrast to the close-up woodland photographs.

title: Budapest Metro: architecture beneath the city
paragraphs: Budapest’s architecture continues underground. During our visit, several metro stations stood out for their design, lighting and strong perspective lines.

Photographing them was challenging. Passengers kept moving through the scenes, and security staff told us we could not use tripods. We had to work around those restrictions and wait for suitable moments.

What interested me most was the relationship between each station and its trains. Older carriages on the older lines made the setting feel consistent with the era in which it was built. In the end, we came away with the photographs we had hoped for.

title: Fisherman’s Bastion in Budapest after dark
paragraphs: Fisherman’s Bastion was one of the places I most wanted to photograph in Budapest. Its pale towers and terraces rise above the city, offering wide views and a setting that feels almost like a storybook.
The architecture was an obvious subject, but the crowds made clear compositions difficult. We waited well into the evening before some of the viewpoints became quiet enough.

By then, blue hour had passed. Instead, we photographed the illuminated buildings against the night sky. The result was different from the pictures I had imagined, but the darker setting suited the towers just as well.

title: Bridges of Budapest: evening photography on the Danube
paragraphs: A September city break gave me time to photograph the bridges connecting Buda and Pest across the Danube. They became some of my favourite subjects in Budapest.
Margaret Bridge offered an interesting steel structure and views towards the island in the river. The Chain Bridge, or Széchenyi lánchíd, was especially compelling once its evening lights came on.

Photographing along the river brought the bridges together with the city’s grand buildings and changing reflections. This collection follows those views as daylight gave way to the illuminated waterfront.

title: Spiral staircases in Paris and Rome: unexpected photo subjects
paragraphs: With little time for photography during city trips to Paris and Rome, I found unexpected subjects inside my hotels: two very different staircases.

In Paris, a traditional wooden spiral staircase suited the classic building around it. At The Hive in Rome, a modern staircase offered a more graphic composition, with a reflection that appeared to continue the pattern across the floor.
Both were reminders to keep looking, even without a planned photo walk. I carried my small Sony RX100 III on these trips, which made it easy to photograph details I might otherwise have missed.

title: Northern Portugal’s Atlantic coast at sunset
paragraphs: During two weeks near Porto, I explored the Atlantic coast between Espinho and the chapel of Senhor da Pedra. Sandy beaches and scattered rock formations offered plenty of subjects for sunset photography.
A wooden walkway followed the shore, linking views along the coast. During my evening walks, it became much quieter than it had been earlier in the day.
I enjoyed photographing both the larger coastal scenes and the way individual rocks shaped the foreground. The changing light made familiar stretches of beach feel different each evening.

title: Capela do Senhor da Pedra: sunset photography on Portugal’s coast
paragraphs: Capela do Senhor da Pedra stands on a cluster of rocks beside the Atlantic, near Porto. During my stay in northern Portugal, this small seaside chapel became one of my favourite subjects.
I photographed it during a colourful sunset, trying several angles as the light changed. The rocks scattered across the beach offered strong foregrounds and helped connect the building with the sea.
The daytime crowds had thinned by the evening, leaving more freedom to explore compositions. These photographs bring together the chapel, the surrounding beach and the last light of the day.

title: A blood moon above an industrial scene in Zoetermeer
paragraphs: For the lunar eclipse in July 2018, I wanted to place the red moon inside an industrial composition. I chose the Boels site near my home in Zoetermeer and framed the moon within the basket of a machine.

Thick clouds left only a brief opportunity to photograph it. The result was not as sharp as I had hoped, but it captured the idea: an unusual celestial event set against a familiar piece of machinery.

title: Dragonflies in the woodland and ponds of Oisterwijk
paragraphs: On the way home from a weekend in Eindhoven, we stopped to walk through the woods around Oisterwijk. Trees and small ponds made a peaceful setting for an unplanned photography stop.
Among the waterside plants, we spotted colourful dragonflies. Photographing them took patience because they rarely stayed still for long.
I eventually caught a blue dragonfly and a red one resting on leaves. These smaller encounters became the highlight of a walk that had begun with the wider woodland landscape.

title: The Dobbe in Zoetermeer: reflections at sunset
paragraphs: While preparing for an InstaWalk in Zoetermeer, I visited the Dobbe near the market square and city hall. This familiar city-centre lake offered more photographic possibilities than I first expected.
Artworks in the water, a wooden bridge and the small park across the lake all provided possible foregrounds. At sunset, their reflections became the main attraction.
Construction work limited some views during this visit, but an interesting sky gave the evening its character. It was a useful reminder to revisit everyday places when the light changes.

title: Dublin and Citywest: a short photography walk
paragraphs: A business visit to Dublin left a little time to explore the city along the River Liffey. Its bridges, older buildings and changing waterfront offered plenty to photograph within a short walk.
The city’s history and more recent development sat close together. I was drawn to that contrast rather than trying to cover every landmark during the limited time available.

We also stayed in Citywest and visited the DCU Ryan Academy. Its unusual, egg-like forms suggested a very different architectural photograph, which I processed with an HDR effect. The academy photograph was taken with permission.

title: Amsterdam at night: canal bridges and the Damrak
paragraphs: I travelled to Amsterdam to photograph its canals around sunset and after dark. Although the city is close to home, I had rarely given myself time to explore its most familiar viewpoints with a camera.

We arrived early to scout a canal composition, then set up an hour before sunset. Several other photographers had the same idea. Passing boats made long exposures difficult, and only a handful of frames worked as intended.

On the way back, we stopped at the Damrak for another view across the water. Between the bridges, canal houses and reflections, the evening offered a reminder of why these busy locations attract so many cameras.

title: Nelson Mandela Bridge in Zoetermeer: lines and light
paragraphs: The Nelson Mandela Bridge spans the A12 in Zoetermeer and was a natural subject for a photography project close to home. Inside, repeated structural lines and changing light created strong perspectives.

I chose black and white for most of the photographs, concentrating on the geometry rather than the bridge’s blue and yellow colours. One toned-down colour image shows a different side of the same structure.
Signs, bins and passing people made clean compositions a challenge. These photographs document the bridge as it appeared during my visit, with its covered walkway and station connections.

title: Riverland Dubai: evening architecture photography
paragraphs: On a return visit to Dubai, I photographed Riverland at Dubai Parks and Resorts. The restaurants, waterfront and themed buildings created the atmosphere of an old European town.
Evening was a good time to explore the light and reflections. The setting felt very different from the high-rise views I had photographed elsewhere in Dubai.

During this visit, security staff told me tripod photography was not permitted. I had already made a few images before putting the equipment away. This collection records that short session and the architectural details that caught my attention.

title: La Mer Dubai: colourful details by the beach
paragraphs: During a March visit to Dubai in 2018, I explored La Mer, then a newly opened beachfront development. The area combined beach views with carefully designed streets, restaurants and small architectural details.

Two subjects stood out: decorative tram tracks running through the urban setting and brightly coloured cabins beside the beach. They offered a different kind of composition from Dubai’s larger landmarks.
Parts of the development were still unfinished during the visit. These photographs capture La Mer at that moment, as people were beginning to discover the new waterfront.

title: Maasvlakte Rotterdam: industrial photography in cold light
paragraphs: The Lyondell chemical plant on Rotterdam’s Maasvlakte had been on my photography list for some time. Its pipes and towers offered a dense industrial composition against the open coastal surroundings.

Finding an unobstructed viewpoint was the main challenge. Much of the area was screened by fences, buildings or other infrastructure. We photographed from a distance and stayed outside the marked areas around the plant.

Strong wind and cold made it difficult to keep the camera steady, especially while taking bracketed exposures for HDR processing. The finished images emphasise the intricate structure that first drew me to the site.

title: Winter in Oosterheem and the Bentwoud, Zoetermeer
paragraphs: A cold spell brought partly frozen water and clear winter light to Oosterheem in Zoetermeer. I photographed the canal around sunset and blue hour, using the ice and reflections as part of the composition.
Strong winds had delayed the freeze, leaving an interesting mix of open water and ice. The familiar neighbourhood looked noticeably different in those conditions.
I also visited the edge of the Bentwoud, where the young trees still left much of the landscape open. Pheasants, rabbits and an unusual foreground detail added to the quiet winter atmosphere.

title: Zoetermeer’s water tower: a return in clear weather
paragraphs: I returned to Zoetermeer’s water tower after photographing it on a rainy day in 2015. This time, clear skies and a Sony A7R II with a Zeiss 16–35 mm lens gave the familiar subject a different appearance.
The tower, known as De Tien Gemeenten, was designed by C. Visser and built in 1927–1928. It stands as a reminder of the period when Zoetermeer was a much smaller town.
Finding a new viewpoint proved difficult because bushes blocked several angles. I ended up using similar compositions to the earlier visit, but the change in weather produced a very different mood.

title: Urbex in Zoetermeer: an office building before demolition
paragraphs: An office building near my home in Zoetermeer was already partly demolished when I photographed it. The short-lived opportunity became my first local exploration of this kind of architectural decay.
Most original details had gone, but broken bicycles offered a foreground. Rainwater had collected on the exposed floors, reflecting the remaining walls and openings.
I used a Sony Zeiss 16–35 mm lens, bracketed the exposures and processed them in Photomatix Pro. The HDR treatment brought out the textures and contrasts.
A sign asking people to keep a room clean remained in a hallway full of debris. That small contradiction became one of the details I remembered most from the session.

title: Sardinia’s Spanish towers: coastal landscape photography
paragraphs: During a visit to southern Sardinia, I photographed one of the historic coastal watchtowers often called Spanish towers. Its position above the shoreline gave the landscape a strong focal point.

I spent time scouting for an angle that connected the tower with the bay rather than isolating it from its surroundings. The relationship between the structure and the coastline was what interested me most.

After sunset, the tower’s outline settled into the darker landscape. These quieter compositions became my favourites from the session, showing how an old landmark can give shape to a wide coastal view.

title: Autumn in the Kaapse Bossen: woodland light and colour
paragraphs: A long walk through the Kaapse Bossen in Utrecht became a study of autumn colour, tree trunks and light filtering through the canopy. The weather was good, and many other walkers were enjoying the woods.
I waited for clear moments between passing visitors and used the Sony 24–240 mm lens for most of the photographs. Longer focal lengths brought the layers of trees closer together in the frame.
Along the way, I also photographed mushrooms on the forest floor. Those small details complemented the wider scenes around the woodland and the De Ruiterberg estate.

title: Texel’s lighthouse: coastal photography between rain showers
paragraphs: Texel’s red lighthouse was a highlight of a weekend on the island. Standing above the dunes, it offered a distinctive subject where the North Sea and Wadden landscape meet.
Rain made it difficult to find a moment to take the camera out. I had also forgotten my tripod, so the long exposures I had imagined were not possible.

Instead, I used the road towards the lighthouse as a leading line and worked with the changing sky. Despite the setbacks, the colours and the lighthouse’s position gave me a series I was pleased to bring home.

title: Capo Spartivento: rocky coves on Sardinia’s southern coast
paragraphs: A short holiday in Sardinia gave me the opportunity to photograph Capo Spartivento. Clear water, a rocky bay and the lighthouse above the coast made it one of the most appealing places I found in the south of the island.
A boat with people snorkelling was in the bay when I arrived. I waited in the sun until it moved out of the composition I wanted.

Without an ND filter, I used Sony’s Smooth Reflections app to combine multiple exposures into a single image. The technique softened the water and helped create the quieter coastal scene I had in mind.

title: Zaanse Schans at dusk: Dutch houses, bridges and windmills
paragraphs: We arrived at the Zaanse Schans in the afternoon to scout locations for an evening photography session. The windmills, traditional wooden houses and waterways offered familiar Dutch subjects, but the daytime crowds made clean compositions difficult.
As the attractions closed and light rain passed through, the area became much quieter. We concentrated on windmills beside the water and the wooden house with a small bridge in front.
Finding reflections was not straightforward. Plants and debris covered parts of the water, so we had to choose viewpoints carefully.
The evening gave us enough photographs that we abandoned our plan for another early-morning session. These images capture the quieter side of the Zaanse Schans as the day came to an end.

title: Eendrachtsmolen and the Rottemeren: a Dutch waterside walk
paragraphs: The Rottemeren are close to my home, but reaching the Eendrachtsmolen took a longer walk than we expected. From where we parked, the windmill stood on the far side of the water.
The walk was worthwhile. The mill, nearby lock and surrounding waterways offered a recognisably Dutch landscape, with several possible foregrounds.
Numerous signs made some angles difficult to simplify. I looked for compositions that kept attention on the windmill and water, using the traditional setting as the main subject of the series.

title: A quiet view of the Noord-AA: long exposures at Sweet Lake
paragraphs: I went to the Noord-AA near Zoetermeer hoping for a quiet waterside composition. My usual spot was occupied, the wind was strong and the warm weather had brought plenty of visitors.
After driving around the lake, I found an empty steel bench. It gave the foreground a clear shape, while the background remained free of buildings and people.
Using Sony’s Smooth Reflections app, I softened the water into a more restful surface. The black-and-white version became my favourite: a simple scene that felt calmer than the busy lake around it.

title: Vlietlanden: long-exposure reflections near Voorschoten
paragraphs: I chose the Vlietlanden near Voorschoten for an evening of long-exposure photography. The Noord-AA was too crowded, so I looked a little further from home for a quieter setting.

Construction work limited the available views, but eventually I found a composition with enough structure to anchor the foreground. Longer exposures flattened the water and strengthened the reflections.

I also experimented with Sony’s Smooth Reflections app. It worked well for the effect I wanted, although the process became much slower as the light faded. The session was as much about learning the technique as finding the location.

title: Zierikzee and Zeeland: historic streets and coastal landmarks
paragraphs: A weekend in Zeeland took me through the historic streets of Zierikzee and out towards the surrounding waters. The town’s old buildings offered a rich contrast with the flat, open landscape around it.

Near Zierikzee, I photographed the Zeeland Bridge across the Eastern Scheldt. Its long, repeating structure gave the water a clear visual rhythm and offered a very different subject from the town centre.

I also visited the Plompe Toren near Koudekerke, a surviving church tower from a village lost to the sea. Together, these locations brought Zeeland’s relationship with water into the photographs: the harbour, the bridge and a solitary reminder of the past.

title: An old car wreck at Plaswijckpark: an HDR experiment
paragraphs: During a family visit to Plaswijckpark near Rotterdam, an old car wreck caught my eye. I did not have my usual Sony A7R II with me, so I used a compact camera instead.

I took three bracketed exposures without a tripod and combined them in Photomatix Pro. A pronounced HDR treatment can easily overwhelm a photograph, but here it suited the worn surfaces and unusual subject.
The result was an unplanned experiment: a small detail from a day out that became worth photographing in its own right.

title: Wilhelminapier Rotterdam: bridges and waterfront light
paragraphs: A short photo walk around Rotterdam’s Wilhelminapier offered views of Hotel New York, the Erasmus Bridge and the wider waterfront. The mix of old and new buildings made it easy to keep looking for another angle.
On the far side of the pier, a pedestrian bridge provided a useful foreground. Further along the Maas, we found a viewpoint towards the Erasmus Bridge and the Euromast.
The sky turned red, although the strongest colour sat away from the bridge itself. We worked with the light that reached each composition and brought home a varied set of waterfront photographs.

title: Scheveningen: beach, pier and sculpture at the shore
paragraphs: Scheveningen is the closest beach to my home and a familiar place to return with a camera. On this visit, I photographed the pier, the Kurhaus and details around the beach.
Near Museum Beelden aan Zee, the sculpture Tsuki-no-Hikari caught my attention. Although visible from the beach, it was something I had not noticed on earlier visits.

Its mysterious form offered a contrast to the larger seaside landmarks. The collection brings those different subjects together, showing how a familiar stretch of coast can still reveal something new.

title: A red evening sky over the Noord-AA, Zoetermeer
paragraphs: When the sky turned bright red, I drove to the Noord-AA in Zoetermeer with my camera. Returning to viewpoints I already knew helped me make the most of a short burst of colour.
The lake’s open water gave the sky room to dominate the scene. Familiar foregrounds and reflections helped hold the compositions together.

The main challenge came during editing. The red was already so intense that pushing it further made the photographs less convincing. I worked to preserve the atmosphere without losing the natural look of the evening.

title: Meijendel in winter: dunes in the last light
paragraphs: My second visit to Meijendel took place in early December. With bare trees, cold air and an early sunset, the nature reserve looked very different from the autumn woodland I had photographed before.
This time, I concentrated on the dunes. The low light brought out their shapes, but the best conditions lasted only briefly.

Protected areas and fences limited where I could walk, so finding a composition took some care. The combination of dunes, forest and nearby beach still made the reserve a rewarding place to explore with a camera.

title: A misty morning at the Rottemeren
paragraphs: I rarely head out for photography early in the morning, but made an exception for a misty visit to the Rottemeren. The lakes are only a short drive from home, making them an appealing place to try something different.
The sun had already risen when I arrived. Even so, fog softened the landscape and gave familiar subjects a quieter atmosphere.

The mist also simplified the backgrounds. A tree on the far bank appeared more isolated because buildings behind it disappeared from view. That change made the morning worthwhile, even without catching the first light.

title: Meijendel near The Hague: woodland, dunes and open sea
paragraphs: Meijendel brings woodland, dunes and beach together close to The Hague. On this visit, the variety of the landscape kept offering new subjects within a single walk.
Trees, grasses and water created intimate scenes inland. Further through the reserve, the dunes opened up and the surroundings became more exposed.
Reaching the broad beach at the end of the walk provided a complete change of scale. This collection follows that progression, from enclosed woodland details to the open sea.

title: Kinderdijk: photographing the Dutch windmills
paragraphs: The windmills at Kinderdijk are close enough to home for a short photography trip. I went to explore the familiar Dutch landscape and find my own compositions along the water.
The weather was unremarkable and the sky lacked the colour I had hoped for. Instead, I concentrated on the windmills, their spacing and their relationship with the surrounding waterways.
One photograph from the session was selected for the Holland Calendar 2017. It was a welcome reminder that a successful landscape photograph does not always depend on a dramatic sky.

title: Den Bosch after dark: squares and waterside reflections
paragraphs: A relaxed visit to Den Bosch gave me time to explore the city and make a few photographs along the way. I had no elaborate plan, just a camera and time to look around.
The illuminated square offered one subject, while the waterways provided another. Clear reflections brought the surrounding buildings into the frame in a different way.
These photographs came from that simple walk: a small collection of evening impressions rather than an attempt to document every landmark.

title: Meerpolder near Zoetermeer: fields, water and SnowWorld
paragraphs: The Meerpolder near Zoetermeer took me a while to appreciate as a photography location. Its open agricultural landscape sits beside the much larger outline of SnowWorld.
The rounded polder, grazing animals and waterways offered quieter subjects than the nearby city. Birds, including storks and egrets, added movement to the fields.
I found that carrying a camera changed how I looked at the area. What first appeared ordinary gradually became a landscape worth revisiting, with both rural details and a recognisable urban edge.

title: Oostpoort Delft at sunset: returning to a personal landmark
paragraphs: Delft’s Oostpoort has a personal meaning for me: it was the setting for our wedding photographs. I returned with my own camera at sunset, hoping to see the historic gate in a different light.

The twin towers and waterside position offered an appealing composition, but conditions were difficult. The sky was fairly plain, algae covered parts of the water and construction work affected the setting.

I made the most of the available angles, while knowing that another visit might offer better conditions. These photographs record one evening at a place I already knew through very different pictures.

title: A fisherman and golden light at the Noord-AA
paragraphs: On my second photography visit to the Noord-AA near Zoetermeer, I returned to the same viewpoint. A fisherman was there again, while the setting sun cast a strong golden reflection across the water.
I used a graduated filter to help control the light and allow longer exposure times. It also introduced noticeable vignetting, which became part of the look of the photographs.
There is some post-processing, but much of the atmosphere came from the light and filter at the time of capture. The combination gave a familiar spot a strikingly different appearance.

title: Dordrecht and the Biesbosch: a city walk and a boat trip
paragraphs: A visit to Dordrecht brought together two very different settings: the historic city centre and harbour, followed by the waterways of the Biesbosch.
The old streets and waterfront made it easy to find compositions. Later, we hired a small boat to explore the nature reserve, where photographing became more of an adventure.

Crossing the river proved difficult, and we briefly became stuck in shallow water before freeing the boat. Despite those challenges, the islands, trees and birds made the Biesbosch a memorable contrast to the city photographs.

title: The HSL near Zoetermeer: finding a frame in concrete
paragraphs: The high-speed railway passes only a few blocks from my home in Zoetermeer. At first glance, the concrete structure seems an unlikely photography subject.

Where the track crosses water, however, its lines and reflections become more interesting. I looked for angles that brought out those relationships rather than treating the railway as something to exclude.
Some careful editing helped shape the finished images. The session was a useful exercise in finding photographic possibilities in everyday infrastructure close to home.

title: Sunset in Oosterheem: a photograph close to home
paragraphs: Interesting clouds sent me out on my bicycle to look for a sunset composition in Oosterheem. I found a bridge on the edge of the neighbourhood with a view across the water.
Without a tripod, I used the bridge to steady the camera. The sun’s reflection helped lead the eye into the scene.
It was a modest, unplanned outing, but I liked the balance of the composition. Sometimes a familiar place and a short window of good light are enough to make a photograph worth keeping.

title: Scheveningen Pier: black-and-white studies during restoration
paragraphs: I photographed Scheveningen Pier while restoration work was underway in 2016. The familiar seaside structure was in a period of change after years of neglect.
Because I visited in the middle of the day, the light was less atmospheric than at sunset. I worked with black and white and HDR processing to emphasise the shapes and textures instead.
The bungee-jump tower became a particularly interesting subject. These images document the pier during that stage of its history, rather than its appearance today.

title: Haarlem and the Spaarne: golden-hour reflections
paragraphs: A weekend in Haarlem gave me time to photograph the old town and the River Spaarne. The Gravestenenbrug was one of the first subjects I explored.
For the golden-hour photograph, I used an older crop-sensor lens on my Sony A7R II so I could fit an ND filter. The longer exposure smoothed the water and recorded movement in the clouds.

I used a Sony 28 mm full-frame lens for the remaining riverside images. Comparing the results was interesting, but the setting itself was the real attraction: bridges, old buildings and quieter corners around Teyler’s Hofje.

title: Amsterdam’s IJ: houseboats and an HDR comparison
paragraphs: After a work appointment in Amsterdam, I walked along the IJ with my camera. It was daytime, I had no tripod and the light seemed fairly ordinary.
One photograph of the houseboats nevertheless became my most popular image on 500px at the time. I had processed it with an HDR effect, which gave it a distinctive appearance.
I still had mixed feelings about the strength of that treatment. This collection includes an unprocessed version for comparison, showing how much editing can change the character of the same scene.

title: New Year fireworks: first photographs with the Sony A7R II
paragraphs: New Year’s Eve 2015 was my first outing with the Sony A7R II, replacing my APS-C Sony A77. I photographed the fireworks from the balcony at home using a 28 mm f/2 lens.
Fireworks were a demanding first subject, but I was pleased with the image quality. The full-frame sensor, resolution and dynamic range were the main reasons I had chosen the camera.
At the time, the E-mount lens range was more limited than it later became. An adapter let me use A-mount lenses, although focusing was slower than I wanted.
The compact 28 mm quickly became a favourite. These pictures mark the start of that change in equipment, as well as the beginning of a new year.

title: Katwijk aan Zee: Christmas sunset on the beach
paragraphs: A Christmas visit to Katwijk aan Zee brought strong winds and a colourful sunset. The open beach offered plenty of room to work with the light and the movement of the sea.
I used longer exposures for some photographs, softening the water into a more painterly surface. The effect contrasted with the rough conditions on the shore.
This short series records the end of that winter day: a familiar Dutch coastline made distinctive by the weather and fading light.

title: A woodland mushroom at Katjeskelder
paragraphs: While visiting my parents at Katjeskelder, I took a walk through the surrounding forest with my camera. I hoped to photograph sunlight falling between the trees.
I could not find a woodland composition that worked, but a colourful mushroom offered a smaller subject instead.
The photograph became a reminder to stay open to a different idea. The image I brought home was not the one I had set out to make, but it still captured something of that walk.

title: Sunset at the Noord-AA: reflections near Zoetermeer
paragraphs: I had visited the Noord-AA many times before taking a camera there. At sunset, the familiar lake near Zoetermeer revealed reflections I had previously walked past without noticing.
I tried several positions around the shore and included a fisherman in some of the compositions. The water carried the evening colour through each scene.

This was also my first experiment with a graduated filter to allow longer exposures. It introduced some vignetting, but that suited the photographs. The outing changed how I looked at a place I already knew well.

title: Oosterheem, Zoetermeer: blue hour beside the canal
paragraphs: I photographed Oosterheem shortly after the neighbourhood shopping centre was completed in 2015. The canal and small park gave the new buildings a setting worth exploring with a camera.
After sunset, the area became quieter. Blue-hour light balanced the illumination from the buildings, while the water added reflections to the composition.
These images are a record of my own neighbourhood at that stage of its development: a small local walk with an opportunity to see familiar surroundings differently.

title: Buytenpark Zoetermeer: Galloway cattle at sunset
paragraphs: The Buytenpark in Zoetermeer has been transformed from a former rubble dump into a green landscape. On this visit, I went out near sunset hoping to photograph the Galloway cattle grazing there.
The animals did not stay still, so the photograph took some patience. Eventually, one paused beside a pond, giving me the foreground I had been waiting for.
The moment was brief. The animal moved towards my camera position afterwards, making the encounter more lively than the finished image suggests. The pond and evening light brought the scene together.

title: The AIVD building in Zoetermeer: an architectural HDR study
paragraphs: The AIVD building in Zoetermeer fascinated me despite its severe appearance. Because it was close to my office, I walked over during a lunch break and photographed it with a Sony RX100 III.
I took a bracketed set without a tripod, then used a strong HDR treatment to emphasise the grey structure. The finished photograph gave it an almost science-fiction character.

The building also held a personal memory. As a student, I had worked there during a holiday job when it housed the Ministry of Education. Carrying papers through its many corridors had given me a very different view of the same place.

title: The Hofvijver in The Hague: reflections of the Binnenhof
paragraphs: The Hofvijver in central The Hague offers a view across the water towards the Binnenhof and the Mauritshuis. I enjoyed returning to this part of the city for its architecture and reflections.
The small island in the pond added a softer detail among the surrounding buildings. Walking around the water gave me several ways to frame the same familiar landmarks.
I photographed this series with a Sony A77 and processed the images in Lightroom and Photomatix. The HDR treatment brought out detail while keeping the reflections central to the scenes.

title: Zoetermeer’s water tower on a rainy day
paragraphs: Zoetermeer’s water tower is one of the city’s distinctive older landmarks. I photographed it on a rainy day in 2015, when the weather gave the building a dark, atmospheric setting.
Designed by architect C. Visser of Delft and built in 1927–1928, the tower offered a contrast with the newer neighbourhoods around it.

I later returned in clear weather with different equipment. Comparing the two visits shows how strongly light and conditions can change a photograph, even when the subject and viewpoint remain similar.

title: Nederlandlaan parking garage: colour, concrete and HDR
paragraphs: After the parking garage beneath my office in Zoetermeer was repainted, I tried photographing its new colours. It was an unlikely subject, but the concrete surfaces offered an interesting test for HDR processing.
The effect brought out colour and texture, particularly around a Tesla Model S in the garage. A familiar, practical space became a more graphic composition.
This small series was an experiment in finding visual interest somewhere I normally passed through without stopping.

title: The windmills at Zevenhuizen in changing weather
paragraphs: I cycled from Zoetermeer to the windmills near Zevenhuizen on two separate occasions. One visit brought sunshine; the other came with a cloudy sky.
The same buildings and waterways took on noticeably different moods. Comparing the photographs showed how much weather can change a familiar Dutch landscape.
Rather than looking for a distant location, these outings made use of a short journey from home. The windmills gave the series a consistent subject while the light supplied the variation.

title: A summer road trip around Iceland: landscapes and waterfalls
paragraphs: We travelled around Iceland in the summer of 2015, making landscape photography the main focus of the journey. The long daylight hours gave us time to explore a remarkable range of scenery.
Waterfalls were a highlight, but the open spaces made just as strong an impression. Even in summer, the cool weather and sparse landscape gave the journey a sense of distance from everyday life.
Looking back, I can see photographs I missed as well as the ones I brought home. That is part of what makes me want to return: the feeling that there is still much more to see.
